opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say my feelings were mixed, which I think is true for most people who work on these models. There was real pride. PaLM 2 was a big team effort, and we made meaningful progress, especially on multilinguality, reasoning, and coding. We also got much better efficiency for the capability level, which mattered a lot because these models were going into real products.

But I wouldn't say I was fully satisfied. When you're close to the work, you see all the places where the model still falls short. It could still make things up. Some reasoning tasks were brittle. And there were things we wanted to try that we simply didn't have time for before the deadline. In this field, by the time a model ships you already know what you'd do differently, and you're already thinking about the next one.

So I was satisfied that it was a solid step forward and that we delivered it. But it felt more like a milestone than a destination. A lot of what we learned from PaLM 2, about data, scaling, and evaluation, fed directly into the work that came after it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I was quite satisfied, and I think the whole team was. PaLM 2 was a big step forward from the original PaLM in a few ways that mattered to us. We trained it on a much more multilingual corpus, so its performance across languages, especially on translation and on tasks in languages other than English, improved dramatically. We also put a lot of work into reasoning, math, and coding, and the gains there were real and measurable.

What I was maybe most pleased about was the efficiency side. We applied compute-optimal scaling, so PaLM 2 was actually a smaller model than the first PaLM, yet it outperformed it on almost everything. That meant it was cheaper to serve and faster at inference, which is what let it get deployed into so many Google products at once. For a research team, seeing your work show up in Bard, Workspace, and so on within weeks of completion was gratifying.

That said, I'm a researcher, so I'm never fully satisfied. There were areas where I knew we had more headroom, like long-context handling, multimodality, and reducing hallucinations. And the field was moving so fast that even as we finished PaLM 2, we were already thinking about what the next generation needed to look like, which eventually became Gemini. So I'd say satisfied, proud, but very aware it was a milestone rather than a destination.
